endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Therefore, CDRH stated that it will be important for manufacturers to consider how to effectively evaluate and monitor the GenAI-enabled device, and the underlying foundation model as applicable, for its specific intended use in a way that can ensure that device accuracy, relevance, and reliability are maintained, once deployed.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Establish policies and procedures for continuous monitoring of third-party GAI systems in deployment.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Building on human factors principles, health systems should: - disable one-click auto-send for higher tiers, - surface uncertainty and missing-context prompts, - force visibility of what the model assumed vs what is chart-verified.

endorsements.title: Adopting and expanding ethical principles for generative artificial intelligence from military to healthcare
endorsements.quote: There must be explicit guidelines for monitoring generative AI systems for potential errors, deactivation to prevent more damage when an error occurs, remedying errors, and interaction to reduce operator errors.

endorsements.title: Large Language Models and User Trust: Consequence of Self-Referential Learning Loop and the Deskilling of Health Care Professionals
endorsements.quote: This acknowledgment underpins the necessity for robust oversight mechanisms, ongoing evaluation of AI-driven outputs for accuracy and relevance, and clear guidelines on its role as an assistive tool rather than a stand-alone decision-maker.

endorsements.title: Recommendations for Clinicians, Technologists, and Healthcare Organizations on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: A Position Statement from the Society of General Internal Medicine
endorsements.quote: Ensure strong internal infrastructure is in place to monitor performance of generative AI, especially in clinical use.

endorsements.title: Embracing Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Research and Beyond: Opportunities, Challenges, and Solutions
endorsements.quote: The dynamic performance of generative AI will necessitate continuous surveillance throughout the use lifecycle.

endorsements.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Academic Surgery: Ethical Implications and Transformative Potential
endorsements.quote: Further, there is a need for careful monitoring of model outputs with specific attention to hallucinations when an AI model generates incorrect or misleading information, often presenting it as fact, and drift, or degradation of the model when production data differs from training data.

endorsements.title: ETHICS of AI Adoption and Deployment in Health Care: Progress, Challenges, and Next Steps
endorsements.quote: Establish continuous monitoring pipelines for model drift.

endorsements.title: Ethical Imperatives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Clinical Nursing: Viewpoint on Responsible AI Use
endorsements.quote: After RAG systems are deployed in clinical practice, they must be regularly assessed for both technical accuracy and ethical impact.

endorsements.title: Integrating Generative AI Into Patient-Centered Clinical Decision Support: Viewpoint on Research and Practice Considerations
endorsements.quote: Monitoring must therefore address behaviors such as hallucinations [ 79 ], reasoning quality [ 80 ], sycophantic behavior [ 81 ], and input robustness or feature drift [ 82 ].

endorsements.title: Responsible and innovative AI for mental health care: five priority themes
endorsements.quote: Post-deployment monitoring should track drift and emergent failure patterns rather than relying on static validation.

evidence.title: Real-world use and evaluation of a generative AI chatbot for Parkinson's disease information: a prospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Conversation-level post-market monitoring detecting critical generative failures
evidence.effect: Monitoring confirmed 5 critical events among 45 flagged and 4 among 100 sampled conversations; failures invisible to automated metrics alone
evidence.quote: Tightly scoped, retrieval-augmented, patient-facing AI achieved favourable automated triage classifications while still harbouring clinically critical failures invisible to automated quality metrics alone; detecting them required conversation-level evaluation with clinical expert adjudication.

evidence.title: Adoption and Use of LLMs at an Academic Medical Center
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations and inaccuracies per LLM-generated summary in the deployed EHR interface
evidence.effect: Estimated 0.73 hallucinations and 1.60 inaccuracies per generation for summaries, the most frequent UI task.
evidence.quote: Generation of summaries was the most frequent task in the UI, with an estimated 0.73 hallucinations and 1.60 inaccuracies per generation.

evidence.title: Retrospective Evaluation of a Generative AI-Enabled Electronic Medical Record System in Primary Health Care Facilities in Kenya
evidence.outcome: Frequency of hallucinations in deployed LLM output
evidence.effect: Hallucinations were uncommon (50/1,469; 3.4%), most often mis-expanded acronyms or drug names.
evidence.quote: Hallucinations were uncommon (50/1,469; 3.4%), most often involving mis-expanded acronyms or drug names.

evidence.title: Multidimensional Assurance of an Electronic Health Record Embedded Generative Artificial Intelligence Summarization Tool
evidence.outcome: Hallucination rate of EHR-embedded generative AI summaries, measured at atomic content unit level
evidence.effect: Hallucination rate 11.79% (95% CI, 11.47% to 12.10%) across 671 summaries containing 40,452 ACUs; the detector agreed with physician adjudication on 96.95% of ACUs in the validation set.
evidence.quote: Across 671 remaining summaries containing 40,452 ACUs, the hallucination rate was 11.79% (95% CI, 11.47% to 12.10%).

evidence.title: Evaluation of electronic health record-integrated artificial intelligence chart review
evidence.outcome: Physician-reported omissions, hallucinations, and confusing content in AI chart summaries
evidence.effect: Among 147 summaries: omissions n=46, confusing content n=20, token limitations n=27, hallucinations n=5, bias n=1; positive feedback n=71.
evidence.quote: Positive feedback was common (n = 71), but users identified omissions (n = 46), confusing content (n = 20), token limitations (n = 27), hallucinations (n = 5), and bias (n = 1).
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated chart summaries with physician free-text feedback (10 physicians)

evidence.effect: Hallucinations in 21% (95% CI 14%-29%), inaccuracies in 41% (53/129; 95% CI 33%-50%), omissions in 24% (31/129; 95% CI 17%-32%) of 129 hospital courses.
evidence.quote: Hallucinations occurred in 21% (95% CI, 14%-29%) of the hospital courses, inaccuracies in 41% (53/129; 95% CI, 33%-50%), and omissions in 24% (31/129; 95% CI, 17%-32%).

evidence.title: Spectral Dynamics of Semantic Drift in Clinical Multi-Agent Language Model Networks
evidence.outcome: semantic drift and hallucination amplification
evidence.effect: Terminal cosine similarity degradation 53.29%; variance amplification 51.81% (ρ= 1.5181) versus ER ρ= 1.0766.
evidence.quote: Moreover, the terminal semantic drift reveals a catastrophic variance amplification of 51.81% ($ρ= 1.5181$) in highly clustered architectures, proving total system unpredictability when compared to Erdős--R'enyi configurations ($ρ= 1.0766$).

evidence.title: Generative and Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Medical Coding and Billing: A Human-in-the-Loop Architecture and Evaluation

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse monitoring deployed generative AI, and one descriptive study of a German deployment found that human review of flagged and sampled conversations detected high-severity failures that automated metrics alone did not reveal. No study compares monitoring with no monitoring or measures its effect on patient harm.

perspectives.view: One descriptive study of 2,035 conversations in a real deployment tests post-market monitoring. It has no comparison group and reports detected events rather than patient outcomes, so certainty is very low. Hazard studies report deployed hallucination rates from 3.4% of records to 21% of hospital courses. These show the problem exists but do not test whether monitoring reduces it.

In the German deployment, reviewers confirmed 5 high-severity events among 45 flagged conversations and 4 among 100 sampled ones. Automated metrics alone did not reveal these failures. In a separate study, LLM judges caught 2 of 9 expert-identified hallucinations. These results suggest that monitoring may need human review and sampling as well as automated flags.

Deployed EHR summarization tools showed 0.73 hallucinations per summary across 1,075 users and a hallucination rate of 11.79% of content units. An automated detector agreed with physicians on 96.95% of units in validation. Automated tools may help triage outputs for review, but another study found that automatic metrics correlated weakly with expert scores (0.10 to 0.23).

The one test included non-English-speaking users and older adults in Germany. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A Kenyan deployment reported hallucinations in 3.4% of records, most often mis-expanded acronyms or drug names. No study has tested whether monitoring detects failures that fall more heavily on these groups.

The FDA CDRH discussion paper calls for monitoring the underlying foundation model where applicable, and NIST AI 600-1 calls for continuous monitoring of third-party systems in deployment. Ten commentaries make similar recommendations. These sources state expectations rather than evidence. No supplied study tested monitoring of vendor foundation model updates specifically.

The German study reviewed 45 flagged and 100 sampled conversations out of 2,035 and confirmed 9 high-severity events. The study summary does not report reviewer time, staffing, or cost. The current evidence therefore does not allow an estimate of what monitoring at scale would require.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares monitoring with no monitoring or links monitoring to fewer errors reaching clinicians or patients. No study tracks drift after vendor foundation model updates in real deployments or reports the staff time and cost of human review. The only study that tests monitoring took place in Germany, and no test of monitoring has been reported from a US health system, although several US studies document the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test included limited English proficiency or non-English users and older adults, but it took place in Germany and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those groups in the United States have no direct evidence that monitoring detects the failures most likely to affect their patients.
